terms.one_line_definition: A computer program that can hold a real conversation, write things, and answer questions the way a person would.
terms.long_definition: AI — short for artificial intelligence — is the umbrella name for software that does work that used to require a human. The kind of AI most people use today (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot) is good with language: reading, writing, summarizing, explaining, brainstorming. Older systems called "AI" were much narrower (a chess engine, a spell-checker); today's AI is broad and conversational, which is why it suddenly shows up in news, products, and meetings everywhere.
terms.why_it_matters: When the news, an ad, or a coworker says "the AI said..." or "AI is going to change everything," knowing what AI actually means lets you cut through the hype and ask the real question: which AI, doing what specifically.
terms.example_in_sentence: I asked the AI to summarize the case notes before our meeting.

terms.one_line_definition: A rough measure of model size — the number of "knobs" the model adjusted during training. Bigger usually means smarter, slower, and more expensive.
terms.long_definition: When you see a model described as "70B" or "405B," that "B" means billion parameters. Parameters are the internal settings a model fine-tuned during training — billions of tiny adjustments that together encode what it knows. More parameters generally mean better answers but slower responses and higher cost per inference. The biggest open-weight models (Llama 405B) and frontier models (Claude, GPT-5) are both in the hundreds of billions of parameters.
terms.why_it_matters: Reading product names like "GPT-5", "Claude Opus 4.7", "Gemini 2.5 Pro", or "Llama 405B" makes more sense once you know that the "B" is billions of parameters. It is the simplest rough comparison of model heft, even though parameters alone do not tell you everything about quality.
terms.example_in_sentence: Llama 3 70B has 70 billion parameters — smaller than Claude but small enough to run on a laptop.

terms.one_line_definition: An LLM hooked up to tools and a planning loop so it can take actions, not just chat.
terms.long_definition: A chat AI just talks back. An agent reads your goal, decides what to do, calls a tool (search the web, run code, send an email), reads the result, decides what to do next, and keeps looping until the job is done. Claude Code is an agent. So is any "AI does the thing for you" product. The pattern is LLM + tools + loop.
terms.why_it_matters: Cross-path with cc-agent — Claude Code calls its specialized helpers "agents" too. The general concept matters because the whole industry is shifting from chatbots to agents. Knowing the term means you can follow that conversation.
terms.example_in_sentence: The agent worked through 30 tool calls before it finished the refactor.

terms.one_line_definition: Large Language Model — the kind of AI that writes, reasons, and chats like a person.
terms.long_definition: An LLM is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama — all LLMs. They can read, write, summarize, code, and converse, and they're the engine behind every modern AI chat product.
terms.why_it_matters: Every "AI" product you use or builds is powered by an LLM. Understanding the term is the foundation for everything else in AI/ML — context windows, tokens, RAG, agents all hang off it.
terms.example_in_sentence: Jargon uses an LLM (Claude Opus 4.7) to grade your free-form sentence answers.

terms.one_line_definition: How often the AI gets the answer right — the share of test questions it answered correctly out of the total.
terms.long_definition: Accuracy is the simplest score on a model's report card. You take a set of test questions where you already know the right answer, run the AI on every one, and count what fraction it got right. If the model answered 87 out of 100 correctly, that is 87% accuracy. It is the first number people look at on a release announcement, and the first number a team checks when something feels off. The catch: accuracy alone can hide problems — a model that always says "no" can still look highly accurate if "no" is the right answer most of the time. That is why teams pair it with other measures.
terms.why_it_matters: Accuracy is the easiest AI quality number to read, which is exactly why it shows up in headlines. Knowing the word — and knowing it is one number out of several — lets you read a model release and ask the next question, which is always "accurate at what, and compared to what?"
terms.example_in_sentence: The new model hit 92% accuracy on the reasoning eval, four points higher than the previous version.

terms.one_line_definition: When an AI confidently makes something up that is not true.
terms.long_definition: AI models generate text that sounds confident even when they do not actually know the answer. Made-up facts, fake citations, invented services — these are hallucinations. They happen because the model is trained to produce plausible-sounding text, not to verify what it says.
terms.why_it_matters: Every AI user gets burned by hallucinations eventually. Knowing the term gives you the right warning to verify anything that matters — citations, code that references libraries, names, dates, numbers.
terms.example_in_sentence: Watch out — that quote is a hallucination, the article never existed.

terms.one_line_definition: Asking the AI to show its reasoning step by step before answering — usually gets a more accurate answer.
terms.long_definition: Chain of thought is when you tell the model to "think step by step" or show its work. The model writes out the intermediate reasoning before the final answer. Counterintuitively, this actually makes answers MORE accurate — the model uses its own written-out steps as scratch space.
terms.why_it_matters: When an AI gets a tricky question wrong, asking for chain of thought is the cheapest fix you can try. It is also why thinking-mode and reasoning-mode features exist in newer models — they bake chain of thought in by default.
terms.example_in_sentence: Adding "think step by step" fixed the math errors — it caught its own mistake.

terms.one_line_definition: A reusable prompt skeleton with placeholders for the parts that change — write it once, fill in the blanks every time after.
terms.long_definition: A prompt template is a prompt you have written carefully ONE time, with placeholders where the variable details go. Something like: "act as a careful editor. read the draft below and give me three pieces of feedback on clarity, tone, and length. draft: {paste here}." The fixed parts (role, instructions, output format) stay the same. Only the input changes. Templates are how people scale up from "I prompt the AI fresh every time" to "I have five prompts I trust and I just plug new content into them." Most AI products that let you save prompts are really just template tools.
terms.why_it_matters: The shift from one-off prompts to templates is the shift from using AI casually to using it as a real tool. A learner who knows the word can recognize the pattern in product features ("save this prompt," "create a custom assistant") and start building their own.
terms.example_in_sentence: Once I had a prompt template for review feedback, I stopped rewriting the instructions every time.

terms.one_line_definition: A model column computed from a DAX expression for each row.
terms.long_definition: A calculated column stores a DAX result for each row of a table in the semantic model. It differs from a measure, which is evaluated dynamically in filter context.
terms.why_it_matters: a calculated column is figured out once per row and frozen into the table, unlike a measure that recalculates with filters. mixing them up is a classic Power BI mistake — using a column where you needed a measure gives you totals that won't move when you slice.
terms.example_in_sentence: We used a calculated column for customer segment because the value never changes once the row is loaded.

terms.one_line_definition: Row-level security that filters model data based on the viewer.
terms.long_definition: RLS stands for row-level security. In Power BI, row-level security applies roles and filters so different viewers can see different rows from the same semantic model.
terms.why_it_matters: RLS is how one report safely shows each person only their own rows — every regional manager opens the same report but sees just their region. when a stakeholder asks "can they see everyone's numbers?", this is the control that answers it.
terms.example_in_sentence: RLS means each regional manager opens the same report but only sees their own region's rows.

terms.one_line_definition: An Excel summary table for grouping, filtering, and aggregating data.
terms.long_definition: A PivotTable summarizes source data by dragging fields into rows, columns, values, and filters. It is commonly used to group and aggregate data without writing formulas for every view.
terms.why_it_matters: when you have thousands of raw rows and someone wants "sales by region by month" in five minutes, a PivotTable gets you there by dragging fields instead of writing a formula for every cell. it's the fastest way to turn a data dump into an answer.
terms.example_in_sentence: I built a PivotTable to group sales by region and month so I didn't have to write a formula for each combination.

terms.one_line_definition: A Fabric workflow for moving or transforming data between systems.
terms.long_definition: A Fabric data pipeline orchestrates steps that copy, transform, schedule, or move data between sources and destinations. Pipelines are often used for repeatable data ingestion and ETL-style workflows.
terms.why_it_matters: a data pipeline is the scheduled plumbing that copies and moves data between systems so nobody's exporting CSVs by hand every night. when someone says "the nightly load," they're talking about a pipeline doing the work while everyone's asleep.
terms.example_in_sentence: The data pipeline copies CRM rows into the lakehouse every night without anyone touching it.

terms.one_line_definition: A one-time update that fills or repairs existing rows.
terms.long_definition: A backfill updates data that already exists. If a new column is added, a backfill might populate it for old rows. If old records used inconsistent labels, a backfill might normalize them. Backfills need care because they touch historical data.
terms.why_it_matters: there's a real difference between changing future behavior and fixing records that already exist. a backfill is the second one, and because it touches historical data it's the kind of job you scope carefully and watch.
terms.example_in_sentence: a pronunciation backfill filled in missing say-it hints for the old acronym terms.

terms.one_line_definition: A query operation that combines related tables.
terms.long_definition: A join lets a query combine rows from multiple tables using a relationship such as a foreign key. If progress rows store only term IDs, a join can pull in the term names and definitions at the same time.
terms.why_it_matters: this is how apps build rich screens out of slim, normalized rows. when a progress record only stores a term id, a join is what pulls in the name and definition so the screen actually has something to show.
terms.example_in_sentence: a dashboard runs a join to show each mastered term right next to your score.

terms.one_line_definition: One record inside a database table.
terms.long_definition: A row is one individual record in a table. In a terms table, one row might be the term "webhook." In a user table, one row might be Alice. Rows hold values for the table's columns.
terms.why_it_matters: it's easy to blur the table (a whole collection) with a single item inside it. keeping "row" as the one-record word is what lets you reason precisely about which exact item a query touched.
terms.example_in_sentence: one row in the terms table is the whole CORS lesson, definition and all.

terms.one_line_definition: A field whose value must be one option from a fixed list.
terms.long_definition: An enum is a controlled list of allowed values. A status might be draft, active, paused, or archived. Enums are useful when free-form text would create drift: "in progress," "In Progress," and "working" all meaning the same thing.
terms.why_it_matters: free-form text drifts fast: "in progress," "In Progress," and "working" all end up meaning the same thing in your data. an enum pins a field to a known set of options so messy vocabulary never becomes messy data.
terms.example_in_sentence: you can make order status an enum so the app only ever stores known states like draft, active, or archived.

terms.one_line_definition: The set of exposed places an attacker could try to exploit.
terms.long_definition: Attack surface is every entry point or behavior someone could probe: public routes, forms, uploads, webhooks, APIs, admin actions, dependencies, credentials, and network boundaries. Reducing attack surface means leaving fewer exposed places to abuse.
terms.why_it_matters: this is the word that explains why every new endpoint, integration, or login option isn't free — each one is another door someone could try. once you think in these terms, deleting an unused webhook or feature stops feeling like cleanup and starts feeling like security.
terms.example_in_sentence: we killed the old webhook nobody used because it just sat there adding to our attack surface.

terms.one_line_definition: Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
terms.long_definition: Encryption turns readable data into unreadable ciphertext using a key. It can protect data in transit, such as HTTPS, or data at rest, such as stored backups. Encryption is reversible only for someone with the right key.
terms.why_it_matters: this is the difference between a stolen laptop being a real problem and being a non-event. when you hear that traffic is "protected in transit" or a backup is safe to store somewhere, this is the mechanism doing the work — and it's also why losing the key can mean losing the data for good.
terms.example_in_sentence: even if someone steals the backup drive, encryption keeps the customer data unreadable without the key.

terms.one_line_definition: Multi-factor authentication, where login requires more than one proof.
terms.long_definition: MFA stands for multi-factor authentication. It asks for two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus an authenticator code, hardware key, device prompt, or biometric check. MFA reduces the damage if one credential is stolen.
terms.why_it_matters: this is why your bank texts you a code after you already typed the right password. knowing the term tells you a system is asking for a second kind of proof on purpose — so if one credential leaks, the account still doesn't fall over.
terms.example_in_sentence: i turned on MFA for my email, so now i need both my password and a code from my phone to get in.

terms.one_line_definition: A protocol for delegated sign-in or delegated access between services.
terms.long_definition: OAuth lets one service grant limited access to another service without sharing the user password with that app. In sign-in flows, the app sends the user to an identity provider such as Google, receives a callback, and exchanges proof for tokens.
terms.why_it_matters: every "continue with google" button is running this under the hood. when you're debugging a login that bounces through a redirect and comes back with a token — or wondering why the app never sees your actual google password — this is the word that makes the whole dance make sense.
terms.example_in_sentence: instead of building our own login, we used OAuth so people can sign in with their existing google account.

terms.one_line_definition: Role-based access control, where permissions are grouped by role.
terms.long_definition: RBAC stands for role-based access control. Instead of checking every user against every action manually, the system assigns roles and checks what each role allows. RBAC is common in admin tools, dashboards, enterprise software, and cloud consoles.
terms.why_it_matters: when an access conversation is going in circles — who can do what, why is this person blocked — naming this is what gets everyone onto the same page. it's the standard pattern in admin tools and cloud consoles, so once you hear it you know access is being handed out by role, not user by user.
terms.example_in_sentence: we set up RBAC so editors can publish posts and viewers can only read them, instead of toggling permissions per person.

terms.one_line_definition: A sensitive credential such as an API key, token, or password.
terms.long_definition: A secret is any value that gives access if someone has it. API keys, service-role keys, database passwords, signing keys, and webhook secrets belong in secret storage, not commits, logs, screenshots, or chat transcripts.
terms.why_it_matters: when someone says "don't ever commit that" about an API key, this is the category they mean. learning to spot one keeps you from the classic mistake of pasting a key into a screenshot, a log line, or a public repo — anything that hands over access just by being seen.
terms.example_in_sentence: that database password is a secret, so keep it in the env file and out of the commit.

terms.one_line_definition: Single sign-on, where one trusted identity provider lets users access many apps.
terms.long_definition: SSO stands for single sign-on. With SSO, a user signs in through a trusted identity provider, and multiple apps rely on that provider instead of each app managing a separate password. SSO often sits beside OAuth, SAML, MFA, roles, and audit logs.
terms.why_it_matters: this is why one work login gets you into email, the dashboard, and a dozen other tools without re-typing a password each time. when names like okta, microsoft entra, or "sign in with your company account" come up, this is the setup they're describing — one trusted provider standing in for every app's login.
terms.example_in_sentence: with SSO set up, employees log in once with their work account and reach every internal app from there.

terms.one_line_definition: A weakness that can be exploited.
terms.long_definition: A vulnerability is a flaw that can be used to break confidentiality, integrity, availability, or trust. It might live in application code, dependencies, configuration, infrastructure, authentication, or business logic.
terms.why_it_matters: when a dependency update is flagged as "security" or a scanner lights up red, this is what it found. knowing the word helps you tell apart a theoretical weakness, a known flaw with a patch waiting, and something actively being exploited right now — which decides how fast you need to move.
terms.example_in_sentence: we shipped the patch the same day because the vulnerability could have leaked private user data.

terms.one_line_definition: A small value the browser stores for a site and sends with later requests.
terms.long_definition: A cookie is a browser-side storage mechanism tied to a site. Servers use cookies to remember sessions, preferences, or tracking IDs. Because cookies are automatically sent back to matching sites, they are useful for login but need careful security settings.
terms.why_it_matters: a cookie is how the browser stays signed in after you refresh the page — the site stored a small value and sends it back on every request. it's tiny and powerful, which is also why it shows up in so many login bugs and privacy settings.
terms.example_in_sentence: the browser sends a session cookie with every request, so the server knows it's still me.

terms.one_line_definition: Metadata attached to a request or response.
terms.long_definition: An HTTP header is extra information sent alongside the main request or response body. Headers can say what format the client accepts, which origin made the request, what auth token is present, whether a response can be cached, or what cookie should be set.
terms.why_it_matters: a ton of invisible web behavior lives in headers: which auth token you're sending, what content type you accept, whether a response can be cached, which origin you came from. when something works in one place and breaks in another, a missing or wrong header is often the reason.
terms.example_in_sentence: i set the authorization HTTP header on the request so the function knows which user is calling.

terms.one_line_definition: The message a server sends back after it receives a request.
terms.long_definition: An HTTP response is the server answering the request. It includes a status code, headers, and often a body: HTML, JSON, an image, or an error message. When the frontend says "the API returned 401," it is talking about the response.
terms.why_it_matters: when a teammate says 'the API returned 401,' they mean the response. it's where the server tells you what actually happened: yes, no, not allowed, not found, try again. reading it is how you stop guessing why a call failed.
terms.example_in_sentence: the call went through but the HTTP response came back with a 403, so the user got bounced.

terms.one_line_definition: A signed token that carries identity or permission claims.
terms.long_definition: JWT stands for JSON Web Token. It is a compact signed string with claims inside, often used to prove who a user is when calling an API. The signature lets the server detect tampering. A JWT is not automatically safe just because it is encoded; it still needs correct expiry, storage, and verification.
terms.why_it_matters: JWTs turn up all over auth logs, edge functions, and Supabase docs. knowing the term makes that plumbing less mystical — and reminds you that being encoded isn't the same as being safe, so it still needs proper expiry and verification.
terms.example_in_sentence: the edge function decodes the JWT to pull out the signed-in user's id.

terms.one_line_definition: The main data carried inside a request, response, event, or token.
terms.long_definition: A payload is the useful contents being transported. In an API request it might be a JSON object. In a webhook it is the event data. In a JWT it is the claims. The envelope is how the data travels; the payload is what the receiver actually needs to read.
terms.why_it_matters: payload is the compact word for 'the actual data inside the thing.' it shows up in API bodies, webhook events, tokens, and logs. once you have it, you can stop saying 'the data part' and just point at what the receiver actually needs to read.
terms.example_in_sentence: the webhook payload had the order id and the amount, so we could match it to the right customer.

terms.one_line_definition: A URL path that an app or server knows how to handle.
terms.long_definition: A route maps a path like `/home`, `/term/:id`, or `/api/cron/ingest-terms` to code that should run. Frontend routes choose screens. Backend routes choose handlers. If a route is missing, the app may show a 404 even though the server is alive.
terms.why_it_matters: a route is the bridge between a URL and a piece of behavior. when navigation breaks, knowing the word lets you say 'that route isn't defined' instead of 'the page is blank' — and a missing route is usually why you get a 404 even though the server is alive.
terms.example_in_sentence: i added a /settings route so that path actually renders a screen instead of 404ing.

terms.one_line_definition: The human-readable site name that points to an internet address.
terms.long_definition: A domain name is the readable name in a URL, such as example.com. DNS translates the domain into an IP address so computers know where to send the request. Domains can point at production sites, preview environments, docs, dashboards, and APIs.
terms.why_it_matters: the domain name is the part of an address that stays recognizable even when paths, query strings, and per-branch preview URLs keep changing. knowing it helps you tell apart 'the site moved' from 'just the route changed' when you're chasing a link.
terms.example_in_sentence: our production domain name stayed the same while the preview URL changed for every branch.

terms.one_line_definition: The numeric summary of how an HTTP request turned out.
terms.long_definition: HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. A status code is the number in an HTTP response that summarizes the result. 200 usually means success, 301 or 302 means redirect, 401 means unauthenticated, 403 means forbidden, 404 means not found, and 500 means the server failed.
terms.why_it_matters: the status code is the fast read on how a call went, and you'll lean on it constantly in network panels, deploy logs, and error reports. 404 means the thing isn't there; 500 means the server fell over — different problems, spotted at a glance.
terms.example_in_sentence: the preview came back with a 404 status code because that route didn't exist.

terms.one_line_definition: A notification that a threshold or failure condition happened.
terms.long_definition: An alert is a notification sent when a system crosses a threshold or detects a failure condition. Good alerts point to something actionable. Bad alerts create noise and teach people to ignore them.
terms.why_it_matters: the difference between a dashboard someone might glance at and a signal that actually wakes a person up is an alert. tuning them matters: too many noisy ones and people start ignoring the one that's real.
terms.example_in_sentence: the alert went off when the checkout error rate stayed above five percent for ten straight minutes.

terms.one_line_definition: Adding or removing compute capacity based on demand.
terms.long_definition: Autoscaling changes the number of running instances, containers, or workers when demand changes. It usually reacts to metrics such as CPU, memory, queue depth, or request volume. It helps absorb spikes without permanently paying for peak capacity.
terms.why_it_matters: this is how a system survives a traffic spike without you paying for peak capacity 24/7. it also explains the lag you sometimes feel under sudden load: new instances take a moment to spin up before they can help.
terms.example_in_sentence: when the queue started backing up during the launch, autoscaling spun up extra workers to catch up.

terms.one_line_definition: Content delivery network: a network that caches assets near users.
terms.long_definition: CDN stands for content delivery network. A CDN stores copies of static assets such as images, JavaScript, CSS, downloads, and sometimes cached responses in many geographic locations. Users fetch from a nearby edge location instead of the origin server every time.
terms.why_it_matters: when images and scripts suddenly load faster after a launch, a cdn is usually why. it also explains a confusing bug: you updated a file but old visitors still see the old version, because a cached copy is sitting at an edge location near them.
terms.example_in_sentence: the screenshots on our landing page got way snappier once we served them through a cdn.

terms.one_line_definition: Putting a version of software into an environment where it can run.
terms.long_definition: A deploy takes code that has been built and puts it somewhere runnable: preview, staging, production, an edge function, a server, or a container service. A deploy is not just saving files; it changes which version a real runtime can execute.
terms.why_it_matters: writing code and getting that code onto a live runtime are two different events, and the gap between them is where a lot of confusion hides. once you can say "it's committed but not deployed yet," you stop wondering why your change isn't showing up on the real site.
terms.example_in_sentence: i pushed the fix an hour ago, but it won't show up until we deploy to production.

terms.one_line_definition: A separate runtime such as local, preview, staging, or production.
terms.long_definition: An environment is one place where the app runs with its own URL, configuration, database, secrets, and safety expectations. Local is for development, preview is for review, staging is production-like testing, and production is what real users see.
terms.why_it_matters: "it works on my machine" almost always means it works in one environment and not another. knowing the word lets you ask the useful question: which environment, with which config and which data, did it break in?
terms.example_in_sentence: the bug only shows up in the staging environment because that's the only place pointed at the real payment provider.

terms.one_line_definition: A system for running and coordinating containers across machines.
terms.long_definition: Kubernetes manages containers across a cluster of machines. It schedules work, restarts failed containers, rolls out new versions, exposes services, and keeps desired state aligned with actual state. It is powerful, but it adds operational complexity.
terms.why_it_matters: when a team says they're "on kubernetes," they're telling you their container operations are a whole discipline, not a one-click upload. that explains why something as simple as a restart can involve schedulers, clusters, and desired state.
terms.example_in_sentence: when that pod crashed overnight, kubernetes restarted it and kept the api up without anyone paging in.

terms.one_line_definition: A recorded event or message emitted by software.
terms.long_definition: A log is a timestamped record that software writes while running: request received, job started, payment failed, retry scheduled, user authenticated. Logs are useful when they include enough context to explain what happened without exposing secrets.
terms.why_it_matters: when something breaks, the log is usually the first place that tells you what the system actually did, instead of what you assumed it did. learning to read it means you stop guessing from the ui and start reading the receipts.
terms.example_in_sentence: the error log showed the webhook came in missing a required field, which is why it kept failing.

terms.one_line_definition: The ability to understand system health from logs, metrics, and traces.
terms.long_definition: Observability is how teams understand what a system is doing from the outside. Logs show events, metrics show numbers over time, traces show request paths, and dashboards or alerts help operators see failures before users report them.
terms.why_it_matters: this is the "can we actually see what happened?" capability, and it's why teams add logs and metrics before things are obviously broken. when an incident hits, the difference between a five-minute diagnosis and a two-hour one is usually whether you set this up first.
terms.example_in_sentence: diagnosing the outage went way faster after we'd added real observability around the checkout flow.
